01.note: The Sages remembered that Rabbi Yehuda bar Elai would take a myrtle branch and dance in front of a bride, calling out 'A fair and attractive bride.' Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak went further and danced juggling three myrtle branches. Rabbi Zeira objected that the old man was making the scholars look foolish. But when Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak died, a pillar of fire separated him from everyone else, an honor said to be given to only one or two people in a generation.
01.why: The Gemara is collecting the songs and praises the Sages offered at weddings and ordinations. This account of dancing before brides belongs to that set, and right afterward Rabbi Zeira concedes that the old man's branch is what earned him his reward.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda bar Elai
people.about: A leading Sage of the generation after the destruction of the Second Temple, remembered here for dancing at weddings.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak
people.about: An elderly Sage, called 'the old man' here, who juggled myrtle branches as he danced before brides.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Babylonian-born Sage who moved to the Land of Israel; at first he disapproved of the juggling.

terms.meaning: A fragrant evergreen shrub; its branches were carried at weddings and celebrations.
A sign of divine honor, recalling the pillar of fire that led Israel in the wilderness. Here it marks someone as one of the greatest people of his generation.
A religious commandment or good deed. Bringing joy to a bride and groom is counted as one.

02.note: A man known as bar Shatya suffered from bouts of insanity, and he sold some of his property. Two witnesses came and said he had sold it while insane, which would cancel the sale; two others said he had sold it while sane. Rav Ashi ruled that the two pairs cancel each other out, so the property stays with bar Shatya. The Gemara adds that this applies only to land he inherited from his fathers; property he had bought himself goes to the buyer, since he may have bought it while insane too.
02.why: The Gemara is asking what happens when witnesses who signed a document are contradicted by others when they are not present. Rav Nahman says to set two against two and leave money with its owner, and cites bar Shatya's sale as his precedent.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A leading Babylonian Sage and judge, who cites this case to support his ruling.

people.name: bar Shatya
people.about: A man with periodic bouts of insanity; his name means roughly 'son of a madman'.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A leading Babylonian Sage, remembered as a chief editor of the Talmud, who ruled on the sale.

terms.meaning: When two witnesses say one thing and two say the opposite, neither pair is believed over the other, so the court acts as if no testimony was given.
Property inherited from one's family. The court presumes it still belongs to the heir unless someone proves otherwise.

03.note: Rav Yehuda tells, and an early teaching confirms, how the marriage contract took its form. At first a groom pledged two hundred dinars to a virgin bride and one hundred to a widow, to be set aside in cash, and men grew old without marrying. The Sages had the money kept in the bride's father's house, but an angry husband could easily say 'Go to your marriage contract.' Then they had it kept in the husband's house, where rich women made it into silver and gold baskets and poor women into a chamber pot, and husbands still said 'Take your marriage contract and leave.' Finally Shimon ben Shatah ruled that the husband writes that all his property guarantees the contract.
03.why: The discussion has been about whether a husband may sell property while it is pledged for his wife's marriage contract; this history explains where that lien on all his property came from.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A leading Babylonian Sage, student of Rav and Shmuel, who reports this history.

people.name: Shimon ben Shatah
people.about: A leader of the Sages in the first century BCE, credited with the final form of the marriage contract.

terms.meaning: The ketuba: a document in which a husband promises his wife a sum of money if he divorces her or dies. It protects her and makes divorce costly.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.
A silver coin; two hundred dinars was a large sum.

04.note: Rabbi Yitzhak asked Rav Nahman why he had not come to the synagogue to pray. Rav Nahman said he was too weak. Rabbi Yitzhak suggested he gather ten men at home to pray; Rav Nahman said that would be too much of a burden on them. Then let the congregation send a messenger to tell you when they are praying, Rabbi Yitzhak said, so you can pray at the same moment. When Rav Nahman asked why he was going to such lengths, Rabbi Yitzhak quoted Rabbi Yohanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai: the 'time of favor' in the Psalm is the time when the congregation prays.
04.why: The Gemara has been quoting Rabbi Yohanan's teachings in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai; this exchange introduces another of them, and other Sages then add their own verses showing the special power of praying with a community.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak
people.about: A Sage of the Land of Israel who urges Rav Nahman to pray together with the congregation.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A leading Babylonian Sage and judge, here too weak to come to synagogue.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The leading Sage of the Land of Israel in the third century, quoted by Rabbi Yitzhak.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai
people.about: A great second-century Sage, student of Rabbi Akiva, whose teaching Rabbi Yohanan passes on.

terms.meaning: A prayer quorum, called a minyan: the ten adult men needed for communal prayer.
A phrase from Psalms 69:14, read here as a moment when God is especially ready to accept prayer.

05.note: Mar, son of Ravina, held a wedding feast for his son and saw that the Sages there were getting too merry. He brought out a precious cup worth four hundred zuz and smashed it in front of them, and they grew sad.
05.why: The Gemara is discussing whether excessive joy is proper; it has just told of Sages rebuked for being too joyful, and follows this with Rav Ashi breaking a glass at his own son's wedding and a mournful song sung at Mar's feast.

people.name: Mar, son of Ravina
people.about: A Babylonian Sage who sobered his son's wedding guests by breaking an expensive cup.

terms.meaning: A silver coin; four hundred zuz was a very large sum.

06.note: Rav Pappa visited the home of Rav Huna, son of Rav Natan. After the meal was over, something more to eat was brought in, and Rav Pappa took it and ate without saying a new blessing. His hosts asked whether he did not hold that once a meal is finished one may not eat again without a blessing. He answered that the rule, correctly stated, speaks of the table being 'removed', not of the meal being finished.
06.why: The Gemara is working out when a meal counts as over, so that further food needs its own blessing; right after, Rava and Rabbi Zeira argue the same question at the Exilarch's house, using Rav Pappa's 'removed' wording.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A Babylonian Sage and head of an academy, a visitor here.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Natan
people.about: A Babylonian Sage, the host of the meal.

terms.meaning: In Talmudic times each diner ate at a small table that was carried away when the meal ended. Taking it away, not just stopping eating, marks the meal's end.

07.note: Rav Adda bar Ahava had a son who was born already circumcised, and the circumcision day fell on Shabbat. He went to thirteen circumcisers, who would not do it, so he did it himself and cut too deep, leaving the boy injured. He said he deserved this for going against the ruling of Rav. Rav Nahman asked whether he had not also gone against Shmuel, who required a drop of blood only on a weekday. The Gemara explains that Rav Adda held such a child certainly has a hidden foreskin, a view Rav Yosef also held against Rabba.
07.why: The Gemara has just reported that Rav and Shmuel disagree whether a baby born circumcised still needs a drop of covenantal blood drawn; this case shows the dispute in practice, and the Gemara goes on to Rav Yosef's proof for his view.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Ahava
people.about: A Babylonian Sage of the third century, the father in this story.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Founder of the great academy at Sura in Babylonia, who ruled that a child born circumcised needs no further cut.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Rav's colleague and head of the academy at Neharde'a, who required a drop of blood to be drawn.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A leading Babylonian Sage and judge, who questions Rav Adda's reasoning.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A Babylonian Sage who held that such a child certainly has a hidden foreskin, so he may be circumcised even on Shabbat.

terms.meaning: A drop of blood drawn from a boy born without a foreskin, in place of a full circumcision, to mark the covenant.
The idea that a baby who looks circumcised may really have a foreskin hidden beneath the skin, so he still needs a circumcision of some kind.
The Sabbath. Circumcision on the eighth day overrides its rest laws, but only when it is certainly required.

08.note: Rav was Rabbi Hiyya's nephew twice over: his father Ayevu was Rabbi Hiyya's half-brother and his mother Imma was Rabbi Hiyya's half-sister. When Rav came up to the Land of Israel, Rabbi Hiyya asked him whether Ayevu was alive. Rav answered by asking whether Imma was alive, and when asked about Imma, asked whether Ayevu was alive. Rabbi Hiyya understood that both had died. He told his attendant to take off his shoes and then to carry his things after him to the bathhouse, and the Gemara draws three rules of mourning from what he did.
08.why: The Gemara is gathering examples of people who avoided saying something unpleasant outright; Rav breaking the news of a death without saying it belongs to that series.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Babylonian Sage who studied in the Land of Israel and later founded the great academy at Sura.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A great Sage who moved from Babylonia to the Land of Israel; Rav's uncle and teacher.

people.name: Ayevu
people.about: Rav's father, Rabbi Hiyya's half-brother.

people.name: Imma
people.about: Rav's mother, Rabbi Hiyya's half-sister.

terms.meaning: News of a relative's death that arrives more than thirty days after it happened. Then one keeps the mourning customs for only one day, not seven.

terms.term: part of the day is like an entire day
terms.meaning: Keeping a mourning practice for even a short part of the day counts as the whole day, which is why Rabbi Hiyya could go to the bathhouse soon after.
A mourner may not wear leather shoes, so Rabbi Hiyya had his removed at once.

09.note: A boat carrying wheat sank in the Hishta River before Passover. Wheat soaked in water may begin to leaven, so it could not be eaten on Passover, and Rava allowed the owners to sell the salvaged grain to gentiles. Rabba bar Levai objected from an early teaching: a garment with an unseen forbidden thread of linen in wool may not be sold to a gentile, because he might sell it on to a Jew. Rava changed his ruling: the owners should sell the wheat to Jews a small amount at a time, so that it would all be eaten before Passover.
09.why: The Gemara has been discussing how carefully grain must be kept from water so it does not leaven before it is baked into matza; this ruling deals with grain that was soaked.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A leading fourth-century Babylonian Sage, whose rulings are usually followed.

people.name: Rabba bar Levai
people.about: A Babylonian Sage who challenged Rava's first ruling.

terms.meaning: The biblical ban on wearing cloth that mixes wool and linen.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.
A small dry measure, roughly a little over a liter.
Non-Jews, who are not bound by the Passover ban on leavened food.

10.note: Ben Kamtzar had a special skill in writing: holding four quills between his fingers, he could write a four-letter word all at once. He refused to teach it to anyone. When asked why, he had no answer, unlike others who had kept their skills secret and could explain themselves. The Sages applied to those others the verse 'The memory of the righteous shall be for a blessing', and to ben Kamtzar and his like 'But the name of the wicked shall rot.'
10.why: The mishna lists Temple craftsmen who kept their skills to themselves, and the Gemara is going through them one by one; just before this it described Hugras ben Levi's secret way of singing. Next it asks what it means for a name to 'rot'.

people.name: ben Kamtzar
people.about: A Temple-era scribe with a unique writing technique that he refused to teach.
